planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; give plenty of room from structures since the narrow, upright form still needs a deep root run.

directions: Italian cypress is the classic, narrow, flame-shaped evergreen of Mediterranean gardens, valued for its dense, dark green, resinous foliage on strongly vertical branches that need almost no shaping to maintain their exclamation-point silhouette. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, since standing water or heavy clay quickly leads to root rot and dieback in this drought-adapted species. Established plants tolerate long dry spells and thrive on minimal irrigation once rooted, but young trees need regular watering through their first one to two summers. In humid climates it can be prone to bagworms and canker diseases, so give it good air circulation and avoid overhead watering.

common_name: Stricta Italian Cypress (Narrow Columnar Mediterranean Cypress)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; space as a row for a formal screen or use singly as a vertical accent.

directions: Stricta is an especially narrow, tightly columnar selection of Italian cypress, often only two to four feet wide even at forty or fifty feet tall, making it one of the most extreme vertical accents available for formal gardens and allees. Grow it in full sun in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil, since it is even less tolerant of soggy roots than the species. It needs little to no pruning to keep its pencil-thin form, though light shearing can tidy any wayward growth. Once established it is very drought tolerant, but in humid or rainy climates watch for cypress canker, which can kill individual branches or whole trees.

planting.note: Plant seedlings or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Arizona cypress is a fast-growing Southwestern native that struggles in heavy, poorly drained soils.

directions: Arizona cypress is a fast-growing, broadly pyramidal native conifer of the desert Southwest, with dusty blue-green to gray-green foliage and shreddy, fibrous reddish-brown bark on older trunks. Plant in full sun in sharply well-drained soil, since it is adapted to dry, rocky slopes and resents wet feet; heavy clay or irrigation-soaked sites invite root and canker diseases. Once established it is highly drought tolerant and needs little supplemental water, making it a popular windbreak, screen, and reforestation tree in arid climates. It grows quickly when young and responds well to occasional light shaping to encourage a dense, well-branched form.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in sharply well-drained soil in full sun; give it room to develop its dense pyramidal form.

directions: Blue Ice is a selection of Arizona cypress prized for its intensely silvery-blue, dense foliage, among the bluest of any hardy conifer, held on a tidy, symmetrical, broadly pyramidal frame. Plant in full sun in sharply well-drained soil, since like the species it is intolerant of standing water and performs poorly in heavy clay. It is markedly drought tolerant once established and needs minimal supplemental irrigation, though young trees benefit from regular watering during their first year or two. Little pruning is required beyond removing damaged growth, and its strong color makes it a popular specimen or screening tree where a cool blue accent is wanted.

planting.note: Plant seedlings or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; site away from irrigated lawns and low spots that collect water.

directions: Smooth Arizona cypress is a central-Arizona native prized for its striking, smooth, exfoliating bark that peels in cherry-red to purple patches over a pale underbark, quite unlike the shreddy, fibrous bark of typical Arizona cypress. It forms a dense, pyramidal tree of gray-green to blue-green foliage and is extremely drought tolerant once established, native to dry, rocky foothill slopes with sharply drained soil. Plant in full sun in lean, fast-draining soil and avoid regular irrigation near the trunk, since excess moisture promotes root and canker diseases. It needs little care beyond removing dead wood and is a popular xeriscape and specimen tree in the Southwest for both its foliage and its ornamental bark.
scientific_name_note: Also classified as Cupressus arizonica var. glabra; some authorities treat it as a variety of Arizona cypress rather than a distinct species.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; in cold climates grow in a large pot that can be moved to bright, sheltered winter protection.

directions: Kashmir cypress is a graceful, weeping conifer from the eastern Himalayas with pendulous branches draped in soft, silvery blue-green foliage, valued as an ornamental in mild climates and as a large container specimen elsewhere; it is the national tree of Bhutan, where it is planted around temples. Plant in full sun in moist but well-drained soil, since unlike the desert cypresses it comes from relatively humid mountain valleys and does not tolerate prolonged drought as well as Arizona or Italian cypress. It has no significant frost hardiness below the mid-20s Fahrenheit, so in temperate zones it is grown as a patio or conservatory plant that summers outdoors and overwinters in bright, cool indoor conditions. Water regularly to keep soil evenly moist and avoid letting the root ball dry out completely.

planting.note: Plant seedlings or container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Nordmann fir prefers cool, moist summers and struggles with heat and drought.

directions: Nordmann fir is a majestic, dense conifer from the Caucasus Mountains with glossy, dark green, non-shedding needles that have made it the most widely grown Christmas tree species in Europe. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, since young trees actually tolerate and often benefit from some shade in their early years, mimicking their native forest-understory start. It prefers cool, humid summers and struggles with prolonged heat or drought, performing best in the Pacific Northwest, upper Midwest, and Northeast rather than hot, dry regions. Keep soil evenly moist during establishment and avoid compacted or poorly drained sites, which lead to root problems over time.

planting.note: Plant grafted container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Korean fir prefers cool, moist conditions and does not tolerate hot, dry summers well.

directions: Silberlocke is a striking Korean fir cultivar whose needles curl upward along the branch, exposing their bright silvery-white undersides in a dramatic two-tone effect that reads almost frosted from a distance. Like the species, it begins producing ornamental cones at a young age, with upright purple-violet cones that fade to blue and brown as they mature against the silver-backed foliage. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist soil in full sun to partial shade, giving it cool, humid conditions similar to its parent species since it does not tolerate hot, dry summers well. It is slow-growing and long-lived, making it a prized specimen conifer for smaller gardens where its unusual color and texture can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Plant grafted container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun.

directions: Candicans is a selection of white fir chosen for exceptionally intense, ice-blue to silvery-white foliage that rivals Colorado blue spruce in color while keeping the softer, more graceful needle arrangement typical of white fir. Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep soil, since like the species it is one of the more drought-tolerant firs and resents consistently soggy roots. Once established it needs only occasional deep watering during extended dry spells, making it a good choice for large landscapes in drier climates than most firs can handle. Give it plenty of room to develop its broad, symmetrical pyramidal form and avoid crowding, which reduces air circulation and lower-branch vigor over time.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist soil in full sun to partial shade; the gold color develops best with several hours of direct sun.

directions: Crippsii is one of the oldest and most celebrated golden hinoki cypress cultivars, forming an open, irregularly pyramidal tree with drooping branch tips and flattened, fan-shaped sprays of rich golden-yellow foliage that hold their color well into winter. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist soil in full sun to partial shade, giving several hours of direct sun daily for the brightest gold tone while avoiding the most intense afternoon exposure in hot climates, which can scorch the foliage. It grows at a moderate pace, slower than the green species, and its graceful, layered branching makes it a long-favored specimen tree in Japanese-style and mixed conifer gardens. Water regularly while young and avoid drought stress or waterlogged soil, both of which dull its color and vigor.

common_name: Ellwoodii Lawson Cypress (Compact Blue-Gray Columnar Falsecypress)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltered from strong wind.

directions: Ellwoodii is a compact, slow-growing, densely columnar Lawson cypress cultivar with soft, feathery, blue-gray juvenile foliage that stays juvenile-textured for the life of the plant rather than maturing to the coarser adult form of the species. Its tight, upright habit and fine texture make it a popular choice for foundation plantings, narrow borders, and containers where full-size Lawson cypress would be far too large. Grow in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade with shelter from strong or drying winds, which can brown the soft foliage. It is notably susceptible to Phytophthora root rot in poorly drained soil, so good drainage is essential, and occasional light shearing in spring helps maintain its dense, conical form.
